title: 1  Introduction
text:
1 Introduction
Simulating the dynamics of deformable solids is essential to fields involving physical interaction, including computer graphics, engineering, and robotics. Furthermore, learning these complex dynamics as predictive physical world models is also considered essential for physical AI. However, fulfilling this vision with traditional simulators remains a fundamental bottleneck: classical high-precision solvers are accurate but slow, and their gradients are hard to obtain. Neural simulation is an emerging alternative: its goal is to learn these complex physical behaviors directly from data, offering fast, differentiable surrogates that bypass the computational bottlenecks of classical solvers ( Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020 ; Pfaff et al., 2021 ) . Nevertheless, high-fidelity deformable simulation demands a high-resolution geometric representation, typically a volumetric mesh with thousands to tens of thousands of vertices. Efficiently and accurately predicting the long-horizon trajectories of such large-scale systems poses significant challenges for conventional neural architectures.
Achieving this, however, presents several tightly coupled challenges. First, high-fidelity 3D volumetric meshes contain large, object-dependent numbers of vertices, resulting in extremely high-dimensional system states. Existing autoregressive (AR) approaches predict the dynamics frame by frame, without jointly modeling the full temporal horizon, and are therefore susceptible to compounding errors and trajectory drift over long rollouts. One-shot prediction of the entire trajectory provides global temporal context, but operating directly at native resolution is computationally prohibitive. Consequently, compressing these complex dynamics into a spatiotemporal latent space becomes necessary, yet largely unexplored for mesh-based volumetric physics. This introduces the first challenge: a representational bottleneck. In our explorations, we find that standard compression methods ( e.g. , with uniform temporal strides and local temporal upsamplers, as in standard video-VAE designs ( Yu et al., 2023 ) ) lose high-frequency temporal information and make reconstructed shapes jump unnaturally, producing a “staircase” artifact that we analyze in Sec. 4 (Staircase analysis). Furthermore, directly compressing raw world coordinates forces models to entangle large-scale rigid motion with millimeter-scale local deformations, severely degrading precision.
The second challenge is the optimal predictive paradigm: it remains an open question whether deterministic regression or generative diffusion is better suited for complex physical simulation, and a systematic comparison in the context of 3D volumetric physics is currently absent. Our systematic experiments reveal a critical insight: microscopic non-determinism can be strongly amplified by the inherently chaotic nature of complex deformable dynamics. For instance, state-of-the-art GPU-based physical solvers ( Huang et al., 2024a ; Huang et al., 2025 ) exhibit only slight microscopic non-determinism, yet chaos can amplify this small difference into vastly different final trajectories (Sec. 4 , Chaos analysis). In this chaotic regime, nearly identical initial conditions can correspond to multiple macroscopically different yet physically plausible futures. Deterministic regression tends to average over these modes, producing damped trajectories that may match none of them, whereas generative diffusion can represent and sample from the multi-modal distribution of plausible outcomes.
To overcome these tightly coupled representational and predictive limitations, we propose PhysLDM, a latent-diffusion paradigm for one-shot volumetric deformable simulation. The foundation of PhysLDM is a novel holistic spatiotemporal variational autoencoder (ST-VAE) specifically designed for mesh-based volumetric physics. By employing a holistic temporal compression strategy and explicitly decoupling rigid body motion from local deformation, our ST-VAE eliminates “staircase” artifacts and preserves fine geometric details. This design achieves a $\sim$ 2.48 mm average geometric reconstruction precision for meter-scale scenes at up to a $78\times$ token compression. By employing a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , PhysLDM models the distribution of physically plausible future trajectories, whereas deterministic regression produces damped averages in our experiments.
A prominent feature of our paradigm is its constitutive-model-agnostic nature. Supervised purely kinematically on an Objaverse-scale dataset, a single PhysLDM demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization capabilities to unseen, out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets. We further demonstrate the utility of PhysLDM as a differentiable simulator for inverse problems and design optimization. To our knowledge, PhysLDM yields the first high-fidelity spatiotemporal autoencoder and latent-diffusion paradigm for volumetric deformable dynamics, offering a scalable and robust approach to neural simulation.
In summary, our main contributions include: • A high-fidelity ST-VAE for 3D volumetric deformable dynamics. We propose a novel holistic temporal compression scheme for volumetric mesh deformable dynamics, which removes the “staircase” artifacts that persist under standard temporal compression. By explicitly decoupling rigid motion and deformation, we achieve $\sim$ 2.48mm average geometric reconstruction precision for meter-scale scenes with up to 78 $\times$ token compression. • A systematic comparison of deterministic regression and generative diffusion paradigms in physical simulation. We reveal that the inherently chaotic nature of complex deformable dynamics can amplify the non-determinism that GPU solvers exhibit under identical initial conditions, and show that in this chaotic regime diffusion is better suited than deterministic regression, whose outputs collapse toward damped averages. • A constitutive-model-agnostic latent diffusion paradigm with strong zero-shot generalization. We present a latent-diffusion paradigm and train a single model, PhysLDM, on Objaverse-scale simulations ( Deitke et al., 2023 ) supervised purely kinematically. Our model transfers zero-shot to unseen OOD object datasets (GSO ( Downs et al., 2022 ) , Toys4K ( Stojanov et al., 2021 ) ) with remarkable robustness. • A differentiable simulator for inverse problems and design optimization. PhysLDM supports end-to-end and higher-order differentiation, enabling efficient material estimation and second-order design optimization tasks that are difficult or computationally prohibitive for existing differentiable simulators.

title: 2  Related Work
text:
2 Related Work
Physics-based deformable simulation. Physics-based Lagrangian simulation has a rich history in computer graphics, evolving from early elastic models ( Terzopoulos et al., 1987 ) to finite element methods (FEM) ( Irving et al., 2004 ) , contact handling ( Bridson et al., 2002 ) , and others ( Müller et al., 2007 ; Bouaziz et al., 2014 ) . Recently, barrier-based methods such as incremental potential contact (IPC) provide strict intersection-free guarantees, but incur high computational costs ( Li et al., 2020 ; Huang et al., 2024a ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2026 ; Ando, 2024 ) . Conversely, real-time solvers achieve interactive rates at the expense of physical fidelity, and they cannot learn the behavior of high-accuracy solvers ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Giles et al., 2025 ) . Differentiable simulators restore gradients, but either require tedious hand-derived formulations or need to backpropagate through every integration step ( Huang et al., 2024b ; The Newton Contributors, 2025 ) . In contrast, PhysLDM serves as a fast, end-to-end differentiable neural surrogate learned directly from high-accuracy solvers.
Neural simulators for deformable dynamics. Neural simulators provide a fast, fully differentiable alternative to traditional solvers. The dominant paradigm of neural simulators is the AR rollout, which predicts the next state frame-by-frame. This paradigm has been adopted across diverse physical simulation fields ( Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020 ; Ummenhofer et al., 2020 ; Pfaff et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . However, AR methods lack the global temporal context necessary for long-horizon consistency, potentially leading to temporal incoherence or trajectory drift. The concurrent work of Chen et al. (2026) performs one-shot multi-frame prediction, but is restricted to low-resolution surface meshes (training on about $356$ vertices per scene) from a limited set of templates ( $35$ different meshes). In contrast, PhysLDM introduces a latent-diffusion paradigm capable of predicting high-resolution volumetric trajectories in a single diffusion pass, demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization to diverse OOD scenes.
Spatiotemporal latent representations. High-fidelity volumetric simulation involves high-resolution meshes, making direct multi-frame prediction computationally prohibitive at native resolutions. However, spatiotemporal autoencoders remain largely unexplored for high-fidelity, volumetric-mesh deformable-body physical simulation. In fact, existing autoencoders for physical simulation typically compress only the spatial domain ( Barbic and James, 2005 ; Fulton et al., 2019 ; Romero et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Chang et al., 2023 ; Modi et al., 2024 ; Liao et al., 2026 ; Wiewel et al., 2019 ; Han et al., 2022 ) , with concurrent neural simulators following a similar pattern ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Geng et al., 2026 ) . While spatiotemporal autoencoders have been successfully deployed in other domains, their architectures are tailored to their respective tasks, such as video generation ( Yu et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) and other fields ( Petrovich et al., 2021 ; Cao et al., 2024 ) . Unfortunately, these designs do not transfer directly to deformable physics. For example, transplanting the standard temporal compression of video VAEs produces severe staircase artifacts (as analyzed in Sec. 4 , Staircase analysis). To our knowledge, our ST-VAE is the first spatiotemporal autoencoder designed specifically for high-fidelity deformable simulation.
Prediction paradigms: regression versus diffusion. For deformable-body physical simulation, deterministic regression and generative diffusion have never been systematically compared. In practice, most work in neural simulation uses regression ( Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020 ; Pfaff et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Dou et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Meanwhile, diffusion ( Ho et al., 2020 ) has instead been adopted where output distributions matter, such as image and video synthesis ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Ho et al., 2022 ) and human motion ( Tevet et al., 2023 ) . Although the concurrent work of Chen et al. (2026) claims that diffusion is superior to deterministic regression, motivated by the diversity of futures under unobserved initial conditions, it never compares one-shot regression with diffusion. By contrast, we systematically compare both paradigms and find that under the chaotic dynamics of complex deformable bodies diffusion is more suitable, and regression may collapse onto non-physical averages.

title: 3.1  Problem Formulation
text:
3.1 Problem Formulation
We formulate the physical simulation of volumetric objects as a trajectory prediction task. Let a scene be represented as a tetrahedral mesh with rest vertices $\mathbf{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}$ . The initial state of the system is defined as $\mathbf{s}_{0}=(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R}_{0},\mathbf{c}_{0},\mathbf{v}_{0},\boldsymbol{\omega}_{0},E)$ , which encompasses the rest geometry, the frame- $0$ pose, linear velocity, and angular velocity, together with the Young’s modulus $E$ of the material. Our goal is to model the distribution $p(\mathbf{X}\mid\mathbf{s}_{0})$ of future vertex trajectories $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times N\times 3}$ over a horizon of $T$ frames. Rather than modeling the raw world coordinates directly, we factor each frame into a global rigid transform acting on a canonical deformation: $\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{R}_{t}\,(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{d}_{t})+\mathbf{c}_{t},$ (1) where $\mathbf{R}_{t}\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $\mathbf{c}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ denote the per-frame rigid rotation and centroid translation, and $\mathbf{d}_{t}$ represents the residual canonical (rigid-free) deformation field. $\mathbf{R}_{t}$ and $\mathbf{c}_{t}$ are extracted from each ground-truth frame in closed form by a per-frame Procrustes (Kabsch) fit of the rest shape ( Umeyama, 1991 ) . This factoring separates the large-scale rigid motion from the small-scale deformation. The rigid transform $(\mathbf{R}_{t},\mathbf{c}_{t})$ carries the global motion in six degrees of freedom per frame. The canonical deformation field $\mathbf{d}_{t}$ then only has to capture the local deformation, which is independent of the object’s pose.

title: 3.2  Architecture Overview
text:
3.2 Architecture Overview
As shown in Figure 2 , PhysLDM has three main modules: a Spatial VAE, an ST-VAE, and an LDM.
Figure 2: Overview of PhysLDM. The framework consists of three main components: (1) A Spatial VAE (top left) that encodes the per-frame canonical mesh into a compact set of resolution-independent latent tokens. (2) An ST-VAE (bottom) that compresses the temporal trajectory into a single joint latent $\mathbf{Z}$ , which serves as the training target of the LDM. (3) An LDM (top right) that predicts the entire latent trajectory from the initial state in a single diffusion pass. Dec $\ast$ denotes the frozen decoders, which decode the latent into the final full trajectory.
Spatial VAE. To efficiently process high-resolution volumetric meshes of varying vertex counts, we compress individual frames using a Spatial VAE. Following the representation of Zhang et al. (2026) , a set of $K$ learnable query tokens cross-attends the canonical mesh vertices to extract a fixed-size set of $K$ latent tokens $\mathbf{z}_{t}$ , which remains independent of the vertex count $N$ . The decoder mirrors the encoder: each rest vertex, embedded with its position, cross-attends the latent tokens and is decoded to its displacement. This module ensures that the latent representation is resolution-independent.
ST-VAE. The ST-VAE compresses the input $T$ -frame trajectory by a factor of $T/M$ into a compact latent $\mathbf{Z}$ . Each frame is represented by $K{+}1$ tokens: the $K$ deformation tokens from the spatial VAE and one additional rigid token that embeds the pose ( $\mathbf{R}_{t}$ and $\mathbf{c}_{t}$ ) in its channels. This token sequence first passes through axial blocks that alternate self-attention across tokens within a frame and along the temporal axis ( Ho et al., 2019 ; Bertasius et al., 2021 ; Arnab et al., 2021 ) , after which it is decoupled into a deformation track and a rigid track. For the deformation track, the standard choice (as in video VAEs) would merge every $T/M$ frames into one latent frame and then decode it with a local temporal upsampler. However, this standard design introduces the staircase artifacts analyzed in Sec. 4 (Staircase analysis). We instead employ a holistic temporal representation where time is summarized by factorized self-attention: for each of the $K$ spatial tokens separately, $M$ learnable queries are prepended to its temporal sequence, attended along the time axis, and kept as the only temporal outputs, giving $K\times M$ tokens in total, which we call holistic temporal tokens. For the rigid track, sharing the holistic tokens with the deformation causes capacity competition and degrades the reconstruction (see ablation in Sec. 4.1 ). The rigid token therefore takes a dedicated linear temporal pathway and recombines with the canonical shape per frame during decoding. Ultimately, the two tracks merge into the single joint latent $\mathbf{Z}$ that serves as the training target of the LDM. The ST-VAE decoder is kept frozen during the LDM stage to decode latents back into full trajectories.
LDM. Conditioned on the initial state, the LDM predicts the latent of the full $T$ -frame trajectory in one pass. The frame- $0$ mesh is injected via cross-attention on its spatial latent, while the pose, the initial velocity, and the stiffness condition the network via adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) alongside the flow timestep. The mesh topology enters only through the frozen decoder, whose graph neural network (GNN) refines the decoded vertices over the tetrahedral mesh. We employ a flow-matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) diffusion transformer (DiT) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) utilizing rectified flow ( Liu et al., 2023 ) to model the probability path. Architecture details are in Appendix A .

title: 3.3  Training
text:
3.3 Training
Our model is trained in three stages. The first stage trains the spatial VAE with a Charbonnier (smoothed $L_{1}$ ) position-reconstruction loss and a Kullback–Leibler (KL) loss (see the spatial-VAE-pretraining ablation in Appendix F ). The second stage trains the ST-VAE on top of the pretrained spatial VAE. Its loss consists mainly of deformation and rigid reconstruction losses over all $T$ frames and a KL loss, together with a latent-anchor loss to the spatial manifold. The third stage trains the LDM on the pretrained, frozen ST-VAE, with a flow-matching velocity mean-squared error (MSE) loss. Complete loss forms, weights, and training details are given in Appendix A .
Constitutive-Model-Free Supervision. Notably, our framework relies entirely on kinematic supervision. Every reconstruction loss is computed directly from geometry, namely vertex positions, velocities, and rigid poses. No constitutive models are used during training or inference. This purely data-driven approach makes PhysLDM agnostic to the underlying simulator’s energy model, allowing it to seamlessly scale across diverse materials, and giving it the potential to learn from real-world captured trajectories where explicit energy models are unavailable (Appendix M ).

title: Data and setup.
text:
Data and setup.
We generate high-accuracy physical simulation data with a GPU FEM solver based on IPC ( Huang et al., 2024a ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . For each scene, we randomly select $n$ objects ( $n\leq 3$ ) from more than $30{,}000$ Objaverse objects, tetrahedralize them with fTetWild ( Hu et al., 2020 ) into volumetric meshes, and assign each object a random initial velocity ( $v_{0}$ ) and a random stiffness (Young’s modulus, $E$ ). The simulation time step is $1/60$ s and each trajectory has $64$ frames. The Objaverse scenes ( $63{,}397$ single-object and $16{,}078$ multi-body trajectories) are split into training, validation, and held-out test sets at a ratio of $90\%:5\%:5\%$ . For OOD evaluation, we generate scenes in the same way from the objects of two other datasets, GSO and Toys4K. The ST-VAE and the LDM are trained on scenes with $N\in[500,5{,}000]$ vertices. The ST-VAE and LDM results in this paper are trained on single-object scenes ( $n{=}1$ ). Our extended model is trained on multi-object scenes ( $n\leq 3$ ; see the multi-body extension in Appendix J ). In the controlled ST-VAE comparisons, we use ST-VAE Small ( $K{=}512$ , $T{=}32$ , $M{=}4$ , $95$ M parameters). In the LDM experiments, we use ST-VAE Base ( $K{=}512$ , $T{=}64$ , $M{=}8$ , $124$ M parameters; Table 3 ). Both configurations compress a trajectory by $8N/513$ in token count, which reaches $78\times$ at the $5{,}000$ -vertex cap. Training details are in Appendix A . Full data details, evaluation setup, and metric definitions are in Appendix B .

title: Staircase analysis.
text:
Staircase analysis.
Standard temporal compression methods (such as video VAEs) uniformly compress consecutive frames into fixed latent blocks along the time axis and decode them with a local temporal upsampler, but this approach is not suitable for 3D volumetric deformable dynamics trajectory reconstruction: it causes the object’s deformation to hold and then snap to the next state, creating an unnatural “staircase” artifact that severely degrades visual fidelity. While this timing error is easily perceptible in video playback, it is difficult to identify from static multi-frame snapshots alone; therefore, we quantify it via the deformation-change correlation (DCC), defined in Appendix B.3 . Although DCC does not solely measure overall reconstruction quality on its own, it plays a decisive role in evaluating the physical plausibility of the motion when reconstruction precision is comparable. A detailed analysis of the staircase artifact is given in Appendix C .

title: Chaos analysis.
text:
Chaos analysis.
Although physics simulators are commonly assumed to produce deterministic trajectories once initial states and parameters are fully specified, this is not guaranteed for GPU solvers. As shown in Fig. 7 , running the same scene five times from byte-identical inputs yields visibly different final poses, with corresponding vertices landing up to $442$ mm apart. This divergence stems from two factors: first, the underlying hardware non-determinism of GPU solvers introduces negligible initial variations; second, the inherently chaotic nature of complex deformable dynamics can rapidly amplify these microscopic errors into macroscopic trajectory divergence. Consequently, training data is not a deterministic function of initial conditions. We also verify this at scale on the $300$ Objaverse held-out scenes: running each scene twice from identical initial conditions, the final-frame vertex trajectories of $23.7\%$ of these meter-scale scenes differ by more than $1\%$ of the object size (about $1$ cm), and those of $7.7\%$ differ by more than $5\%$ (about $5$ cm) (Table 5 ). This chaotic nature suggests why regression models struggle: faced with multiple branching futures, a squared-error loss would drive the model toward the conditional mean, collapsing incompatible outcomes into a damped and non-physical average. A generative approach like our LDM naturally avoids this by sampling plausible trajectories. A more detailed chaos analysis is given in Appendix D .

title: ST-VAE Reconstruction Results.
text:
ST-VAE Reconstruction Results.
Table 1 and Fig. 3 evaluate our holistic ST-VAE against two alternative designs: standard temporal compression (the design of video VAEs) and a direct world-coordinate baseline (which applies holistic compression without the factoring of Eq. ( 1 )). All models share a matched compression rate and are assessed across the same three evaluation sets (Appendix E ). The results yield three primary observations. First, holistic temporal compression eliminates staircase artifacts. Standard compression suffers from the staircase artifact (Sec. 4 , Staircase analysis), which shows up as its clearly lower DCC. Our holistic ST-VAE preserves accurate motion timing, achieving a DCC exceeding $0.93$ across all evaluation sets. Furthermore, augmenting the standard baseline with auxiliary velocity or spectral losses, or placing the latent frames adaptively in time, does not mitigate this limitation (Table 7 ). Second, decoupling rigid motion from deformation enhances precision. The direct world-coordinate baseline underperforms the holistic ST-VAE across all deformation and rigid motion metrics, and shows noisy and cluttered geometric detail in the visual comparison (Fig. 3 ). Third, the holistic ST-VAE achieves superior precision across diverse scenarios. Under up to $78\times$ compression, the ST-VAE yields a mean geometric reconstruction error of just $2.48$ mm on held-out scenes, representing about half the error of the standard baseline, with a median vertex error below $2$ mm. It achieves the best performance across nearly all metrics and datasets, except for one rigid-rotation entry where it is a close second. This performance holds robustly zero-shot on OOD sets like GSO and Toys4K, where its errors stay at the same level as in distribution, and on high-resolution meshes exceeding the $5{,}000$ -vertex training cap, where its mean error is still only a few millimeters. The least accurate held-out cases, geometries with many long, thin features, are analyzed in Appendix I .

title: Prediction Results.
text:
Prediction Results.
Table 2 and Fig. 4 compare three models predicting a $64$ -frame trajectory from the same initial state: our LDM, a capacity-matched deterministic regression model (both using one-shot prediction and the same ST-VAE), and a frame-by-frame AR graph network based on MeshGraphNets (MGN) (Appendix E.3 ). Because complex deformable dynamics are inherently chaotic, world-space error alone is insufficient to evaluate prediction quality, as the ground truth represents only one of many valid outcomes. Therefore, Table 2 primarily relies on physics-consistency checks (Appendix B ; the full set of checks is in Table 8 ). Across all metrics and datasets, the LDM significantly outperforms both baselines. We highlight three observations from the results. First, the LDM consistently outperforms deterministic regression in generating physically plausible trajectories. The regression model produces damped outputs with geometric artifacts and jitter (e.g., $22.7\%$ volume violations versus $7.9\%$ for the LDM on held-out scenes). In contrast, the LDM reduces these artifacts and better preserves the deformation-to-rigid energy ratio. Second, one-shot prediction provides the global temporal context necessary to prevent the compounding errors typically seen in autoregressive models. Consequently, the AR baseline drifts over time and accumulates nearly three times the world-space error of the LDM ( $80.6$ against $28.2$ mm). Third, this strong performance transfers zero-shot to OOD datasets (GSO and Toys4K), demonstrating the robust generalization of our approach. Finally, the LDM remains highly efficient, running at $40$ to $80$ frames per second on a single GPU, even for high-resolution meshes exceeding the training cap (Appendix G ).

The diffusion results in Table 2 use a single sample per scene, which cannot show whether diffusion captures the several possible outcomes of a chaotic scene. To test whether diffusion benefits from modeling several outcomes, we compare the two models separately on chaotic and non-chaotic held-out scenes and draw eight diffusion samples per scene (Appendix D.6 ). Diffusion outperforms regression on both subsets. One may worry that this only reflects a stronger model. However, the diffusion samples spread much more widely on the chaotic scenes, and this spread follows the difference between two runs of the solver. Since the model is the same on both subsets, this effect comes from the generative paradigm and not from a stronger model. A soft key dropped onto the ground illustrates it (Fig. 8 ). Run twice, the solver lets the key fall over in two different directions. Every diffusion sample faithfully falls toward one of the two correct directions, while regression predicts a non-physical average that matches neither run.

title: ST-VAE.
text:
ST-VAE.
We remove the ST-VAE and let a DiT of the same capacity as our LDM denoise the vertex $\times$ frame tokens directly (Table 9 ). Without the latent, one-shot diffusion at native resolution is computationally prohibitive. Memory per sample grows with the vertex count. Even on a $140$ GiB H200, the model at batch $1$ runs out of memory at $2{,}600$ vertices. With the latent, the LDM works on a fixed number of tokens and its cost is independent of the vertex count. The vertex-dependent cost moves to the ST-VAE stage, whose training memory grows linearly with $N$ (Table 9 ), so on the same GPU the training cap rises from about $2{,}500$ vertices without the latent to about $14{,}000$ for ST-VAE Base. The latent also improves the quality of the generated geometry. A raw-coordinate model predicts every vertex directly, so any noise left by the sampler shows up as per-vertex jitter. Our model decodes all vertices from the latent, so the same noise only shifts the shape slightly and coherently (illustrated in Appendix L ).

title: The dedicated rigid pathway in ST-VAE.
text:
The dedicated rigid pathway in ST-VAE.
In the ST-VAE (Sec. 3.2 ), the rigid token bypasses the holistic temporal compression and takes its own linear temporal pathway. To test this design, we route the rigid token through the shared holistic temporal compression instead. In our experiments, this one change causes two failures: the translation error explodes, and the reconstructed deformation shrinks drastically (detailed diagnostics in Appendix F ). Further ablations (spatial-VAE pretraining and the decoder GNN) are reported in Appendix F .

title: Material Estimation.
text:
Material Estimation.
The bottom-right block of Fig. 1 shows a material estimation task. Given a single simulated trajectory of a body with unknown stiffness, we recover its Young’s modulus $E$ by gradient descent through the model, since the mismatch to the observed trajectory is differentiable in $E$ end to end. Because Young’s modulus is usually measured on a logarithmic scale, we optimize $E$ in $\log_{10}$ space, where an error of $1$ dex means a factor of $10$ . To cover a wide range of stiffness, we repeat the task on seven bodies with moduli from $3\times 10^{4}$ to $3\times 10^{6}$ Pa, each starting from an initial guess up to $1.1$ dex away. In all seven cases, our model recovers $E$ within $0.06$ dex in $40$ Adam steps, which takes about $40$ seconds per run. DiffIPC solves the task only after its solver parameters are tuned by hand, and then needs $26$ minutes on $48$ threads. Newton/Warp fails in the backward pass, because backpropagating through its enormous number of substeps explodes the gradient.

title: Beyond Material Estimation: Designing the Throw.
text:
Beyond Material Estimation: Designing the Throw.
Based on the first task, we may ask a further question: which throw reveals the stiffness best, so that the estimation above becomes easier? Easier means that a change of $E$ produces a larger change of the trajectory, so the trajectory carries more information about the stiffness. We therefore maximize the sensitivity of the predicted trajectory to $E$ over the release velocity by gradient ascent through the model. The objective is a derivative, so its gradient is a second-order quantity. Our model supports higher-order derivatives through the automatic differentiation of PyTorch, so it provides this gradient directly, and $30$ Adam steps finish the design in $7$ minutes. Replayed in the ground-truth simulator, the optimized throw makes the rigid motion $13\times$ more sensitive to the stiffness. DiffIPC offers only first-order derivatives and cannot be applied directly to this second-order task. A workaround is to obtain the second-order gradient by nested finite differences, but then DiffIPC is about $635\times$ slower than our model per gradient step. The whole design would take several days, which is not acceptable in practice. Newton/Warp does not produce a usable first-order gradient on this scene, so a second-order one is out of reach.

title: 5  Conclusion
text:
5 Conclusion
We introduce PhysLDM, a latent diffusion paradigm for predicting the dynamics of high-fidelity volumetric deformable bodies. To overcome the computational limits of processing high-resolution meshes, we developed a novel holistic ST-VAE that explicitly disentangles global rigid motion from local deformations. This architecture eliminates the staircase artifacts inherent to standard temporal compression, ensuring highly accurate trajectory reconstruction even for high-resolution, out-of-distribution meshes. Operating on this compact latent representation, we demonstrate that while deterministic regression produces damped, non-physical averages in this chaotic regime, our generative approach predicts physically consistent trajectories in a single diffusion pass. Finally, trained purely kinematically, PhysLDM delivers robust zero-shot generalization and provides end-to-end differentiability, unlocking complex inverse design optimizations that remain intractable for traditional solvers.
Limitations and Future Work. Currently, our model focuses on predicting $64$ -frame trajectories in a single diffusion pass. Extending this one-shot approach into an autoregressive framework presents a promising direction for future research.

text:
Appendix
§A specifies the architecture, losses, and training of all three stages. §B gives the data, evaluation setup, and metric definitions. §C details the staircase analysis of standard temporal compression. §D the chaos experiment on a traditional GPU simulator. §E describes the baselines. §F collects further ablations. §G reports inference runtime. §H shows additional qualitative results. §I analyzes the extreme cases. §J the multi-body extension. §K the setup and results of the differentiable applications. §L the comparison with concurrent work. §M tests the constitutive-model-agnostic property on a second energy model and on real captured trajectories.

title: A.1  Stage 1: Spatial VAE
text:
A.1 Stage 1: Spatial VAE
The spatial VAE is an $8$ -layer transformer of hidden width $512$ ( $44$ M parameters). Its input is one frame in canonical coordinates, i.e. the rest shape plus the deformation $\mathbf{d}_{t}$ of Eq. ( 1 ) with the rigid motion removed. The encoder cross-attends $K{=}512$ learned query tokens against the $N$ vertex tokens of the frame and outputs $K$ latent tokens of width $D{=}48$ , independent of $N$ . We denote the latent of frame $t$ by $\mathbf{z}_{t}$ . The decoder mirrors the encoder: the $N$ rest vertices, embedded with their positions, cross-attend the latent tokens and are decoded back to their $N$ displacements. The decoder additionally takes the mesh topology as input, because a shallow GNN over the tetrahedral mesh then refines the decoded displacements. The spatial VAE is trained first with a Charbonnier position loss and a KL term.

title: A.2  Stage 2: ST-VAE
text:
A.2 Stage 2: ST-VAE
The per-frame latents $\{\mathbf{z}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ are processed by a stack of factorized space–time attention blocks ( Ho et al., 2019 ; Bertasius et al., 2021 ; Arnab et al., 2021 ) . The holistic temporal compression then summarizes the time axis: $M$ learned query tokens attend over each spatial token’s $T$ -frame sequence, and only these $M$ outputs are kept as the temporal representation, while the $T$ per-frame outputs are discarded. The rigid-motion token bypasses this attention compression and is compressed by a separate linear temporal path. The two are kept apart because the rigid signal is orders of magnitude larger than the deformation and, when the two share one compression path, takes over the shared latent and starves the deformation track (Sec. 4.1 , Appendix F ). The two tracks then merge: the joint latent is $\mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times(K+1)\times D}$ of Sec. 3.2 , i.e. $M$ temporal tokens for each of the $K$ deformation tokens and the rigid token, each of width $D{=}48$ . The decoder mirrors the encoder: per-frame queries attend over the $M$ temporal tokens to recover a latent for every frame, which the spatial VAE decoder turns into vertex positions. Table 3 lists the two ST-VAE configurations used in this paper, ST-VAE Small for the controlled comparisons of Table 1 and ST-VAE Base for the LDM experiments (Sec. 4 ). Both configurations compress a trajectory by the same factor, counted in tokens. The input has one token per vertex per frame, $T\times N$ tokens in total, and the latent has $M\times(K{+}1)$ tokens. Since $T/M{=}8$ and $K{+}1{=}513$ in both configurations, the token compression ratio is $8N/513$ , which reaches $78\times$ at the $5{,}000$ -vertex cap.

title: A.3  Stage 3: LDM
text:
A.3 Stage 3: LDM
The LDM and the regression model receive the same conditioning: the frame- $0$ spatial latent through cross-attention, and the initial pose, the initial velocity $v_{0}$ , and the Young’s modulus $E$ through adaptive layer normalization. The LDM is a DiT with $12$ blocks of width $768$ ( $170$ M parameters) operating on the $4{,}104$ latent tokens of ST-VAE Base ( $M\times(K{+}1)=8\times 513$ tokens of width $D{=}48$ ). It is trained with rectified flow and sampled by Euler integration. The regression model is a capacity-matched transformer that emits the full latent trajectory in one pass. Training the spatial VAE, ST-VAE Base, and the LDM takes about $7$ days in total on $8$ H200 GPUs.

title: A.4  Loss details
text:
A.4 Loss details
All position losses use a Charbonnier penalty on the per-vertex error norm, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{charb}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{x})\;=\;\frac{1}{|V|}\sum_{i\in V}\sqrt{\lVert\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{i}\rVert^{2}+\epsilon^{2}},\qquad\epsilon=10^{-3}\ (=1\,\mathrm{mm}),$ (2)
Stage 1: Spatial VAE. $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{S1}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{charb}}+\beta_{1}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}$ with a standard Gaussian KL term and $\beta_{1}=10^{-5}$ .
Stage 2: ST-VAE. The objective combines the deformation reconstruction of all $T$ frames, the rigid track, and a KL term: $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{S2}}=\sum_{j\in\{\mathrm{deform},R,c\}}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}e^{-s_{j}}\mathcal{L}_{j}+\tfrac{1}{2}s_{j}\Big)+\beta_{2}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\mathrm{fb}},$ (3) where $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{deform}}$ is $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{charb}}$ averaged over the $T$ decoded frames, $\mathcal{L}_{R}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{c}$ are mean-squared errors on the rigid token’s rotation and translation, and the three are balanced by the learned uncertainty weights $s_{j}$ of Kendall et al. (2018) . $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\mathrm{fb}}$ is the KL term with per-channel free bits ( Kingma et al., 2016 ) .
Stage 3: LDM. The latent is standardized per modality (rigid and deformation channels separately). With flow time $\tau$ , noise $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})$ and the straight path $\mathbf{x}_{\tau}=(1{-}\tau)\mathbf{z}+\tau\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ , the LDM minimizes a token-weighted velocity regression $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DiT}}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\Big[\big\langle w_{k}\,\lVert\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{k}-(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{z})_{k}\rVert^{2}\big\rangle_{k}\Big],\qquad w_{k}=\begin{cases}\lambda_{\mathrm{rigid}}&k\ \text{a rigid token}\\ \lambda_{\mathrm{deform}}&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}$ (4) where $k$ indexes the $(K{+}1)\times M$ latent tokens and $\lambda_{\mathrm{rigid}}$ is a hand-tuned weight that up-weights the rigid token relative to the deformation tokens ( $\lambda_{\mathrm{deform}}{=}1$ ). The regression model minimizes the same token-weighted mean-squared error directly on the latent.

title: B.1  Data details
text:
B.1 Data details
All simulation data are generated with StiffGIPC ( Huang et al., 2025 ) , a GPU IPC solver. IPC solvers are widely adopted in scenarios that demand high simulation accuracy, such as embodied AI ( Kim et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Such a solver runs offline. Learning its behavior and turning it into a fast, fully differentiable neural simulator is therefore of practical importance. All 3D meshes used for training come from the Objaverse dataset ( Deitke et al., 2023 ) . Each asset is voxel-remeshed to a watertight surface, tetrahedralized with fTetWild ( Hu et al., 2020 ) , reduced to its largest connected component, and rescaled to a unit bounding box. Meshes with more than $10{,}000$ vertices are discarded, and the ST-VAE and the LDM are trained on scenes with $500$ – $5{,}000$ vertices. Every scene drops one meter-scale solid onto a ground plane. The object is released with its lowest point $0.85$ to $1.65$ m above the ground. Each object receives a random initial velocity $v_{0}$ and a random stiffness $E$ (a horizontal $v_{0}\sim U(0,2)$ m/s and a Young’s modulus $E$ log-uniform in $[3\times 10^{4},3\times 10^{6}]$ Pa) under a Stable Neo-Hookean material. Multi-body scenes follow the same setting with two or three objects, each with its own $E$ and $v_{0}$ , thrown toward each other so that they collide in mid-air before reaching the ground. In total, the dataset contains $63{,}397$ single-object and $16{,}078$ multi-body simulated trajectories. The simulation time step is $1/60$ s, and each trajectory has $64$ frames. Held-out scenes are excluded from all three training stages, and every reported number is computed on these held-out scenes or on the OOD sets. For OOD evaluation we generate $1{,}015$ GSO and $3{,}814$ Toys4K scenes under the identical simulation setting. They never appear in training.

title: B.2  Evaluation setup
text:
B.2 Evaluation setup
(a) ST-VAE reconstruction (Table 1 ). For each evaluation set (held-out, GSO, Toys4K), we randomly draw $300$ scenes with $500\leq N\leq 5{,}000$ vertices for the main columns and $300$ scenes with $N>5{,}000$ vertices for the large-mesh columns. Every model is evaluated on the same scenes. (b) Prediction (Table 2 ). The same $300$ scenes per set within $500\leq N\leq 5{,}000$ . The LDM uses $50$ Euler steps. Every metric is a per-scene value, reported as the median across scenes to limit the influence of a few extreme values.

title: B.3  Metrics of Table  1
text:
B.3 Metrics of Table 1
• DCC (deformation-change correlation): the deformation change of a trajectory at frame $t$ is the mean vertex displacement between two consecutive frames in canonical (rigid-free) coordinates, $v(t)=\mathrm{mean}_{v}\lVert\mathbf{d}_{t+1,v}-\mathbf{d}_{t,v}\rVert$ , where $\mathbf{d}_{t,v}$ is the position of vertex $v$ in the deformation field $\mathbf{d}_{t}$ . The deformation-change curve is $v(t)$ over the trajectory. DCC is the Pearson correlation between the deformation-change curves of the reconstruction and of the ground truth. It is reported as the mean across scenes. It detects the staircase artifact directly, since holds suppress the speed and snaps spike it. This metric is amplitude-invariant, so it does not reflect reconstruction quality on its own and should be considered together with the other metrics. • Recon (geometric reconstruction error; mean / med / P90): the encode–decode error of the deformation field, i.e. the per-vertex Euclidean error of the rigid-free deformation $\mathbf{d}_{t}$ averaged over vertices and frames of a scene (mm). The three columns are the mean, median, and 90th percentile across scenes. The 90th percentile reflects the hardest $10\%$ of scenes. For the direct world-coordinate baseline, which has no deformation field of its own, a rigid transform is fitted to each output frame by the Kabsch algorithm, and the residual after removing it is scored as the deformation error. • rot (rotation error): the geodesic $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ distance between the predicted and ground-truth per-frame rotation (relative to frame $0$ ), averaged over the frames of a scene and then over scenes (degrees). For the direct world-coordinate baseline, the rotation and translation are those of the per-frame fitted rigid transform. • trans (translation error): the centroid translation error (relative to frame $0$ ), averaged over frames and then over scenes (mm).

title: B.4  Metrics of Table  2
text:
B.4 Metrics of Table 2
All of these metrics are computed from the predicted and ground-truth trajectories alone and do not require knowledge of the underlying constitutive model. The violation rates are defined as follows. A physical quantity (speed or acceleration) is computed for every vertex at every frame, once from the prediction and once from the ground truth. Each such vertex-frame pair is one sample. A sample is counted as a violation if the predicted value is more than twice, or less than half, the ground-truth value. The violation rate is the fraction of violated samples. Samples whose ground-truth value is too small to be meaningful are excluded by a magnitude threshold. • Volume viol. (volume violation rate): this measures whether the prediction preserves volume where the ground truth does. For every tetrahedron at every frame, we compute how much its volume differs from its rest volume, once in the ground truth and once in the prediction. We look only at the cases where the ground truth changes the volume by less than $3\%$ , because there the ground truth preserves volume. Among these cases, a violation is one where the prediction changes the volume by more than $10\%$ . The rate is the fraction of violations. • Self-int. (self-intersection rate): the percentage of surface triangles of the tetrahedral mesh that cross another surface triangle, averaged over frames and reported as the median across scenes. The ground truth has no self-intersection in any frame, so its value is $0$ . • Vel. viol. and Acc. viol. (velocity and acceleration violation rates): the violation rate of the per-vertex speed and acceleration magnitudes. The acceleration threshold excludes free fall and settled frames. • $KE_{\mathrm{def}}/KE_{\mathrm{rig}}$ (deformation-to-rigid kinetic energy ratio): a rigid transform $(\mathbf{R}_{t},\mathbf{c}_{t})$ is fitted to every frame by the Kabsch algorithm, which gives the rigid trajectory $\mathbf{r}_{t,v}=\mathbf{R}_{t}\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{v}+\mathbf{c}_{t}$ of the rest shape $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$ . The vertex velocity $\mathbf{v}_{t,v}$ (central difference of $\mathbf{x}_{t,v}$ ) is split into the rigid velocity $\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{rig}}_{t,v}$ (central difference of $\mathbf{r}_{t,v}$ ) and the deformation residual $\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{def}}_{t,v}=\mathbf{v}_{t,v}-\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{rig}}_{t,v}$ . With lumped vertex masses $m_{v}$ and the impact window $W$ ( $\pm 10$ frames around first contact), the two kinetic energies are $KE_{\mathrm{def}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{t\in W}\sum_{v}m_{v}\lVert\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{def}}_{t,v}\rVert^{2},\qquad KE_{\mathrm{rig}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{t\in W}\sum_{v}m_{v}\lVert\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{rig}}_{t,v}\rVert^{2},$ and the reported value is $(KE_{\mathrm{def}}/KE_{\mathrm{rig}})_{\mathrm{pred}}\,/\,(KE_{\mathrm{def}}/KE_{\mathrm{rig}})_{\mathrm{GT}}$ , taken as the median across scenes. Scenes where the ground truth barely deforms (deformation below $1\%$ of the kinetic energy) are skipped. At impact, the kinetic energy of the object is divided between the motion of the object as a whole and the internal motion that deforms it. How much goes into deformation depends on how soft the object is and how hard it hits. The ground truth gives the correct proportion for the same object and the same impact, so comparing the two ratios shows whether the prediction moves energy into deformation the way the GPU solver does. A value below $1$ means the prediction deforms less than the ground truth and moves more rigidly. A value above $1$ would mean unphysical deformation or jitter. In Table 2 every model is below $1$ , and the regression model is the lowest on all three evaluation sets, consistent with the damped averages discussed in Sec. 4 . • World err (world-coordinate error): the per-vertex Euclidean error in world coordinates against the ground-truth trajectory, averaged over vertices and frames, reported as the median across scenes (mm). Because deformable dynamics are chaotic, the ground truth may be only one of many possible outcomes, so this number is a reference and not a full measure of prediction quality.

title: C.1  Symptom and diagnosis
text:
C.1 Symptom and diagnosis
Figure 5: The staircase artifact on five GSO scenes. Top: ground truth at the impact frame. Bottom: deformation-change curve (defined in Appendix B.3 ) for ground truth and the six ST-VAEs of Table 7 over the impact window. DCC in Table 1 is the correlation of this curve with the ground-truth curve. On every scene the standard baseline, its two variants, and the adaptive-compression baseline stay below ground truth for several frames and then overshoot it in one frame, while the holistic ST-VAE follows the ground-truth curve. The direct world-coordinate baseline also follows the ground-truth curve, because it uses the same holistic temporal compression.

The standard baseline and its two variants change much less than the ground truth for the first three pairs and then much more in the last two: the reconstruction holds and then snaps. The direct world-coordinate baseline, which uses the holistic temporal compression, follows the ground truth until the last pair.

The symptom is wrong timing of rapid motion. Where the ground truth changes quickly, for instance at impact, the reconstruction holds its shape for several frames and then jumps to catch up, so the motion arrives late and all at once. We diagnose it in three ways. Fig. 5 plots the deformation-change curve on five scenes. The curves of the standard baseline, its two variants, and adaptive compression stay below ground truth for several frames and then overshoot it in one frame. The holistic ST-VAE follows the ground truth, and so does the direct world-coordinate baseline, which uses the same holistic temporal compression. Fig. 6 shows the same behavior directly on the silhouettes of one scene. The silhouettes of the standard baseline and its variants change less than the ground truth for three frames and then more than it in the last one or two frames. Adaptive compression changes less than the ground truth over all five frame pairs and releases the motion even later. The direct world-coordinate baseline follows the ground truth until the last pair. Table 4 scores the five scenes with DCC. The holistic ST-VAE is the best or tied on every scene.

title: C.2  Cause
text:
C.2 Cause
In the standard baseline, the decoded frames at the latent-frame positions are accurate, and the frames between them carry the error. The most likely cause is that standard compression summarizes every $k$ frames into one latent frame and loses the high-frequency temporal information that says when, within those $k$ frames, the rapid change happens. One might think that the problem is a mismatch between neighboring blocks. This is not the case. Two observations show that the error builds up inside each block. First, the standard baseline moves too little during the early frames of every block and then catches up in the last frames, whereas the ground truth moves at a steady pace throughout the block. Second, smoothing the reconstruction across block boundaries does not remove the artifact.

title: C.3  Why the variants and adaptive compression do not help
text:
C.3 Why the variants and adaptive compression do not help
The two variants of the standard baseline and the adaptive-compression baseline all keep the approach of standard temporal compression: they compress the trajectory into a fixed number of latent frames and then reconstruct the frames by local temporal upsampling, so they leave the artifact in place. The velocity loss and the spectral loss change the training signal only. The standard baseline still cannot place the rapid change at the right instant between two latent frames. Adaptive compression moves the latent frames toward the impact, which makes the steps fewer but steeper. A likely reason is that the rebound and settling phases are left with one or two latent frames, so their motion is released in a late snap. The direct world-coordinate baseline uses the holistic temporal compression and shows almost no staircase. Its high DCC in Table 4 together with its lower precision in Table 1 shows that its weakness is precision rather than timing.

title: D.1  Setup
text:
D.1 Setup
We take one held-out scene, a soft tennis racket dropped onto the ground, and run the GPU solver five times on the same GPU from byte-identical inputs: the same tetrahedral mesh, initial state, material parameters, and solver configuration. To measure how far two runs drift apart at a given frame, we compute the displacement of every vertex between the two runs and report the largest one as a fraction of the object’s extent.

title: D.2  The perturbation is tiny
text:
D.2 The perturbation is tiny
The non-determinism of the solver is real but minute. After the first simulation step the five runs differ by at most $0.02$ mm, two hundred-thousandths of the object size. Before the racket reaches the ground, the runs still differ by at most $3\%$ of the object size, mostly in the strings of the net, and their centres of mass by less than $1$ mm. Until the racket reaches the ground, the five runs are therefore practically identical.

title: D.3  Amplification after impact
text:
D.3 Amplification after impact
The behavior changes qualitatively at impact. After the racket hits the ground, the runs diverge rapidly and settle into visibly different poses (Fig. 7 ). Over the ten pairs of runs, the final divergence ranges from $10\%$ to $51\%$ of the object size, with a median of $21\%$ . The same vertex can land up to $442$ mm apart in two runs.
To check that this is chaos and not a peculiarity of the reduction order, we replace the rounding noise by a controlled perturbation: a deterministic initial rotation of the racket between $10^{-8}$ and $10^{-2}$ rad. The final divergence is of the same order for every magnitude and does not grow with it. A perturbation a million times larger does not produce a larger difference. This is the signature of chaotic dynamics. The racket has several possible resting poses. Even the smallest perturbation is already enough to change which one it ends in, so making the perturbation larger does not make the difference larger. It only changes which resting pose the racket lands in.

title: D.4  Where the chaos comes from
text:
D.4 Where the chaos comes from
The sensitivity comes from complex dynamics involving contact. When the racket hits the ground, the solver makes a discrete decision about which edge or corner touches first, and a microscopic perturbation can flip this decision. From then on the bounce and the final pose follow different paths. In our experiments, soft objects that are thin, branchy, or non-convex are more prone to amplifying this chaotic effect.
Figure 7: Chaos in a traditional GPU simulator. Five reruns (columns) of the same soft-racket scene from byte-identical inputs (same mesh, initial state, material, and solver configuration), shown at four sampled frames (rows): before the drop, just after impact, mid-bounce, and the last frame of the trajectory. The runs are indistinguishable until impact and then settle into visibly different poses. The complex dynamics are chaotic, so the post-impact outcome is not a deterministic function of the initial state.

title: D.5  How common is chaos across scenes?
text:
D.5 How common is chaos across scenes?
The racket above is a single scene. To measure how often two runs of the solver diverge, we run the GPU solver a second time from byte-identical inputs on all $300$ Objaverse held-out scenes of Table 1 and compare the two runs. We measure their difference relative to the object size, defined as the diagonal of the bounding box at frame $0$ . Table 5 counts the scenes whose difference exceeds $1\%$ , $5\%$ , and $10\%$ of the object size, using either the mean per-vertex error over the whole trajectory or the per-vertex error at the last frame.
Most scenes are reproduced closely. The median difference between the two runs is $0.5$ mm over the trajectory and $1.0$ mm at the last frame. A substantial minority of scenes, however, diverge. At the last frame, about a quarter of the scenes end more than $1\%$ of the object size apart, and the most divergent scene ends $35\%$ apart. In all of these scenes, the two runs agree to sub-millimeter precision until ground contact and separate afterwards, as in the racket example. A difference of $1\%$ of the object size means that the two runs end more than $1$ cm apart on a meter-scale object, which is already a large error for high-precision physical simulation. A regression model can only learn the mean of such diverging outcomes, so high precision is difficult to reach on these scenes.

title: D.6  Regression versus diffusion on chaotic and non-chaotic scenes
text:
D.6 Regression versus diffusion on chaotic and non-chaotic scenes
In a chaotic scene, the same initial state can lead to several different outcomes. A regression model gives one prediction per initial state, while a diffusion model can draw several. This section tests whether, on chaotic scenes, the samples of the LDM actually cover the different outcomes that the solver produces. We split the $300$ held-out scenes of Table 5 by how far the two solver runs end apart: $71$ chaotic scenes, whose runs end more than $1\%$ of the object size apart, and $229$ non-chaotic scenes. For every scene we draw eight samples from the LDM and report two numbers: the error of a single sample, and the error of the best of the eight samples. Choosing the best sample needs the ground truth, so the best-of-eight result is an upper bound on sample selection, not a usable predictor. All other settings follow Table 2 .
Table 6: Regression versus diffusion on the $229$ non-chaotic and the $71$ chaotic held-out scenes (two solver runs ending less or more than $1\%$ of the object size apart). Medians over scenes. Vol.: volume violation rate (%), KE: $KE_{\mathrm{def}}/KE_{\mathrm{rig}}$ relative to the ground truth, Err: world-coordinate error (mm) (Appendix B.4 ). Best of $8$ picks, per scene, the sample closest to the ground truth. Non-chaotic ( $229$ scenes) Chaotic ( $71$ scenes) Vol. $\downarrow$ KE $\to$ 1 Err $\downarrow$ Vol. $\downarrow$ KE $\to$ 1 Err $\downarrow$ Regression $12.6$ $0.72$ $25.0$ $38.4$ $0.69$ $63.2$ Diffusion, single sample $3.8$ $0.82$ $18.0$ $25.4$ $0.75$ $54.0$ Diffusion, best of $8$ $4.4$ $0.83$ $14.6$ $22.8$ $0.79$ $44.7$
Diffusion outperforms regression on both subsets. Table 6 shows that a single diffusion sample already improves on the regression model in every metric, on both subsets. It has a lower error than the regression model in $79\%$ of the non-chaotic scenes and $65\%$ of the chaotic scenes. The advantage of diffusion is therefore not limited to chaotic scenes.
Multiple samples matter more under chaos. What differs between the two subsets is how much the eight samples add over a single one. Picking the best of the eight lowers the median error by $3.4$ mm on the non-chaotic scenes and by $9.3$ mm on the chaotic scenes. The samples also spread further apart under chaos: the gap between the best and the worst sample of a scene is $7$ mm on the non-chaotic scenes and $25$ mm on the chaotic scenes (medians over scenes). On the chaotic scenes, this spread follows the physics. It grows with the distance between the two solver runs (Spearman $\rho=0.38$ , $p=0.001$ ), and the second solver run lies inside the spread of the eight samples in $99\%$ of the scenes. The benefit does not depend on picking the best sample: averaged over the eight samples, the median final-frame error on the chaotic scenes is $138$ mm, below the $162$ mm of the regression model. The diffusion model is thus more uncertain where the physics is less predictable, and this uncertainty covers outcomes that the solver itself produces.
An example: a falling soft key. In a scene with several possible outcomes, diffusion can learn these outcomes, whereas regression can only learn a non-physical average that matches none of them. Fig. 8 shows such a scene, a soft key. When the solver is run twice, the key falls over in two different directions. The regression model predicts a single pose that lies between the two runs and resembles neither. The eight diffusion samples instead fall on both sides, and the closest of them come close to each of the two runs. Other scenes behave similarly. Among the six scenes whose two runs end more than $30^{\circ}$ apart, at least one diffusion sample ends within $30^{\circ}$ of a solver run in five scenes, while the regression model does so in only one.
An advantage of the paradigm, not of a stronger model. One may worry that the diffusion model is simply the stronger model (the LDM uses $50$ sampling steps, the regression model a single pass), and that the results above reflect this difference. Three observations show that on chaotic scenes the advantage comes from the paradigm. First, the diffusion samples differ from each other in a way that follows the physics: their spread grows with the distance between the two solver runs and contains the second run in $99\%$ of the chaotic scenes. A deterministic model, however strong, gives a single prediction per initial state and has no such spread. Second, where the solver itself produces clearly different outcomes, the diffusion samples reach them, while the regression prediction is a non-physical average between them, as in the key example. Third, the benefit of drawing several samples depends on the scenes, not on the model. With the same model on both subsets, it is almost three times larger on the chaotic scenes ( $9.3$ against $3.4$ mm), whereas a difference in model strength would affect both subsets alike.
In summary, diffusion predicts more accurately than regression on both chaotic and non-chaotic scenes. On chaotic scenes it also produces several plausible outcomes, while regression gives a single non-physical average result. These results show that diffusion is better suited to chaotic deformable dynamics.

title: E.1  Reconstruction baselines (Tables  1  and  7 )
text:
E.1 Reconstruction baselines (Tables 1 and 7 )
All reconstruction baselines use the $8\times$ temporal compression rate and the $T{=}32$ window of ST-VAE Small, start from the same pretrained spatial VAE (except the direct world-coordinate baseline), and are trained on the same data with comparable budgets. • Standard : standard temporal compression of video VAEs. It stacks per-frame latents $\{\mathbf{z}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ and shares the factorized spatiotemporal attention of our ST-VAE, but downsamples time by strided convolution to $T_{\mathrm{lat}}=T/k$ latent frames and reconstructs the full frame rate from this time-ordered sequence of latent frames with a local temporal upsampler. • + velocity loss : the strongest variant of the standard baseline we found. It adds a velocity-matching loss on the consecutive-frame differences of the reconstructed deformation and an unfrozen spatial VAE. • + spectral loss : the standard baseline with an additional loss on the deformation-change curve of Appendix B.3 . The curve is transformed along the time axis with a Fourier transform, and the energy at each frequency is compared with that of the ground-truth curve. Low frequencies correspond to slow changes of the deformation and high frequencies to fast ones, so the loss asks the reconstruction to contain as much fast change as the ground truth instead of smoothing it away. It fails possibly because a frequency spectrum records how much fast change there is but not when it happens, so the standard baseline still cannot place the rapid change at the right instant between two latent frames. • Adaptive compression : a separate baseline that keeps the number of latent frames of the standard baseline but places them non-uniformly along time according to the temporal curvature of the ground-truth deformation. Its lower DCC in Table 1 may have the following cause. With only $M{=}4$ latent frames per $32$ -frame window, the impact takes most of them and the rebound and settling frames are left with one or two, so their motion is likely reconstructed flat and released in a late snap. • Direct world-coord. (direct world-coordinate reconstruction): removes the factoring of Eq. ( 1 ). Its spatial VAE is trained on world-coordinate frames without canonicalization, and the same holistic temporal compression is applied on top without a rigid token, so rigid motion and deformation share one latent.

title: E.3  Prediction baselines (Table  2 )
text:
E.3 Prediction baselines (Table 2 )
The prediction baselines receive the same initial state as PhysLDM. • Regression : a deterministic regression model that is capacity-matched to the LDM and shares its ST-VAE and conditioning. It is a transformer that emits the full latent trajectory in one pass and is trained with the token-weighted mean-squared error of Appendix A , so that only the predictive paradigm differs between the two. • MGN-style AR (MeshGraphNets-style autoregressive model): a graph network ( Pfaff et al., 2021 ) over the tetrahedral mesh graph that predicts one frame at a time from the previous frames, with the noise-injected one-step training standard in that family ( Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020 ) , retrained on our scenes. Predicting world coordinates step by step, it accumulates error over time and drifts far from the ground truth (Table 2 ). It is compared with our model under a fair setting.

title: E.4  Full prediction results (Table  8 )

title: F.1  The ST-VAE
text:
F.1 The ST-VAE
This section gives the measurements behind the ST-VAE ablation of Sec. 4.1 , which asks what happens to the training cost when the ST-VAE is removed and the LDM denoises the raw vertex $\times$ frame tokens directly. We compare two options on the same GPU at increasing vertex counts $N$ . The first is our LDM architecture applied to the raw tokens, without any latent. The second is our pipeline with the ST-VAE, where the LDM works on a fixed set of $4{,}104$ latent tokens and the ST-VAE is the stage with the largest memory footprint. Table 9 lists the peak training memory of both.
Without the ST-VAE the number of tokens is $T\times N$ , so memory grows with $N$ . The raw-token model fits at batch $1$ up to $2{,}500$ vertices and runs out of memory at $2{,}600$ , below the median resolution of our dataset ( ${\sim}3{,}400$ vertices). More than half of the training scenes therefore cannot be processed at all. With the ST-VAE, the LDM costs about $4.4$ GiB per trajectory at any $N$ . The ST-VAE stage grows linearly with $N$ , by about $8$ GiB per $1{,}000$ vertices, and ST-VAE Base trains up to about $14{,}000$ vertices on the same card. The latent therefore does not remove the vertex-dependent cost, but moves it to a stage that scales far more gently.

title: F.2  The rigid pathway
text:
F.2 The rigid pathway
Sec. 4.1 shows that routing the rigid token through the shared holistic temporal compression makes the translation error explode and starves the deformation track: on a small held-out diagnostic set, the translation error grows from $1.8$ to $887$ mm, and the reconstructed deformation shrinks to $28\%$ of its true magnitude ( $97\%$ with the dedicated pathway). In addition, the failure is not a matter of numerical scale. Normalizing the rigid signal to unit variance before the shared compression barely helps ( $52.8\!\rightarrow\!49.6$ mm world error), whereas the dedicated linear pathway reaches $8.3$ mm. The rigid and the deformation signals compete for the capacity of the shared latent, and the dedicated pathway removes this competition.

title: F.3  Spatial VAE pretraining
text:
F.3 Spatial VAE pretraining
This section explains why the spatial VAE needs to be pretrained first rather than trained directly together with the ST-VAE. We compare two training schemes at a matched budget. The first pretrains the spatial VAE and then trains the ST-VAE on top of it with an additional latent-anchor loss (Sec. 3.3 ), which ties the per-frame latents reconstructed by the ST-VAE to those of the pretrained spatial VAE. The second trains both stages jointly from scratch, with a randomly initialized spatial VAE.
We find that joint training works poorly. At the standard learning rate, training diverges within a few thousand steps. At a reduced learning rate, it converges to a much worse model: the geometric reconstruction error is about $5\times$ that of the pretrained scheme, the deformation is much weaker than the ground truth, and volume is lost. The likely reason is that the two stages chase each other. The latent that the ST-VAE learns to reproduce keeps moving while the spatial VAE is still changing, so the temporal model has no fixed target. Pretraining fixes the target first. Once pretrained, the spatial VAE can either be kept frozen during ST-VAE training or fine-tuned with a smaller learning rate, and the two options give similar results. We keep it frozen for ST-VAE Small and fine-tune it for ST-VAE Base.

title: F.4  The spatial decoder GNN
text:
F.4 The spatial decoder GNN
We use a GNN component in the spatial VAE decoder because the field decoder places every vertex independently, so nothing ties neighboring vertices together, and the GNN over the tetrahedral mesh adds this coupling. We compare three placements of the GNN: in the decoder, as in our model; removed; and moved to the encoder instead. Without the GNN, reconstruction degrades and many mesh edges end up stretched far from their rest length. With the GNN in the encoder, the result is worse on every metric, because smoothing the mesh before encoding removes detail before it reaches the latent, whereas smoothing after decoding only regularizes the output.

title: Appendix G  Inference Runtime
text:
Appendix G Inference Runtime
This section reports the inference speed of PhysLDM and how it depends on the mesh resolution. We measure batch-1 inference on a single H200 for $64$ -frame trajectories on five held-out scenes with $980$ to $9{,}851$ vertices, the last three beyond the $5{,}000$ -vertex training cap. One inference pass consists of three steps: the spatial VAE encodes frame $0$ , the latent model predicts the latent trajectory (one forward pass for the regression model, $50$ or $20$ Euler steps for the LDM), and the ST-VAE decodes all $64$ frames. Timings are medians over repeated runs with the GPU synchronized and no I/O in the timed region, in bf16 and in fp32 . Table 10 lists the decoding time, the resulting frame rates, and the peak GPU memory.
Two observations follow. First, the cost of the latent model is independent of the mesh resolution, because it always works on the same $4{,}104$ latent tokens, so its latency is the same at every $N$ ( bf16 : $9.8$ ms for the regression model, $460$ ms for the LDM at $20$ steps, and $1{,}150$ ms at $50$ ). The decoder is the only stage whose cost grows with $N$ , and in bf16 it is nearly flat, from $318$ ms at $980$ vertices to $384$ ms at $9{,}851$ , with no loss of accuracy. As a result, the LDM runs at about $40$ to $80$ frames per second in bf16 and the regression model at up to $195$ , even on meshes twice the training cap. Second, the whole pass needs only about $5$ GiB of GPU memory across the range.

title: Appendix I  Extreme Cases Analysis
text:
Appendix I Extreme Cases Analysis
This section analyzes extreme cases. The accuracy of the LDM is fundamentally bounded by the reconstruction performance of the ST-VAE, meaning that the most challenging cases for the ST-VAE set the limits of the entire pipeline. Across the held-out scenes, the largest reconstruction errors mostly occur on geometries with many long, thin features.
Fig. 12 illustrates a representative extreme case, a soft birdcage comprising $9{,}021$ nodes, which is $1.8$ times the $5{,}000$ -vertex training cap and contains dozens of thin bars only a few tetrahedra thick. Its mean reconstruction error over the trajectory is $9.9$ mm, about twice the held-out mean for meshes above the training cap (Table 1 ). This error is localized to the thin bars, which exhibit distorted and tangled reconstructions. Nevertheless, the overall shape of the collapsed cage, its pose, and its motion over the trajectory are all recovered.
Furthermore, node count alone is not the primary performance bottleneck. For instance, the teaser mug shown in Fig. 1 represents a compact solid with $11{,}621$ nodes ( $2.3$ times the training cap) yet achieves a lower reconstruction error of $5.3$ mm. What distinguishes the birdcage is the density of thin features that deform independently of each other. The folding of every bar is a high-frequency deformation, and the fixed-size latent has to carry it for dozens of bars at once. The latent has enough capacity for the global shape, but not for the fine detail of every bar.

title: Appendix J  Multi-Body Extension
text:
Appendix J Multi-Body Extension
This section describes the multi-body extension of our method and presents its qualitative results. Our approach generalizes effectively to multi-object scenes. The factorization defined in Eq. ( 1 ) is applied at the scene level: a single global rigid transform $(\mathbf{R}_{t},\mathbf{c}_{t})$ is fitted across the vertices of all bodies, while the relative motion among bodies is captured by the canonical deformation field $\mathbf{d}_{t}$ . Because the spatial VAE encodes all vertices within a scene through a shared set of $K$ query tokens, multi-body scenes are encoded, compressed, and predicted in the same manner as single-body objects, requiring no architectural modifications to the ST-VAE or the LDM.
We train both the ST-VAE and the LDM on scenes containing up to three bodies ( $n\leq 3$ ), where randomly selected objects are thrown toward each other to collide in mid-air before hitting the ground. Each body is assigned an independent random Young’s modulus and initial velocity.
Fig. 13 illustrates the ST-VAE reconstruction on four multi-body scenes across four representative frames: immediately before and after the mid-air collision, the first frame following ground impact, and the final settled state. All bodies within each scene, including their collisions and ground contacts, are successfully reconstructed through the single global transform. Fig. 14 demonstrates one-shot prediction on four multi-body scenes conditioned on the initial state, with predictions rendered using the original textured assets. The entire scene, encompassing each individual body along with its collision dynamics and landing behavior, is predicted end-to-end in a single diffusion pass.

title: K.1  Material estimation
text:
K.1 Material estimation
The first task is to recover the Young’s modulus $E^{\star}$ of a body from a single observed trajectory. Because $E$ enters our model through the scalar material channel, the mismatch between the predicted rollout and the observation is end-to-end differentiable with respect to $\log E$ . Starting from initial guesses up to 1.1 dex away from seven ground-truth moduli $E^{\star}\in[3{\cdot}10^{4},3{\cdot}10^{6}]$ , our model successfully recovers all seven within $0.06$ dex in just 40 Adam steps ( $\sim$ 40 seconds). Figure 15 compares the observed, initial, and recovered trajectories and shows the estimation error across all seven moduli.
Figure 15: Basic material estimation. (a) Four matched time samples of the observed trajectory ( $E^{\star}=60$ kPa), the initial model prediction ( $E_{0}=250$ kPa), and the prediction after 40 Adam steps ( $\hat{E}=52.4$ kPa). All views share the same camera and scale. (b) Absolute log-stiffness error for seven ground-truth moduli, with the illustrated case highlighted in blue. All seven final estimates are within $0.06$ dex; each optimization takes approximately 40 seconds. Curves show the recorded iterates without smoothing.
Existing differentiable simulators already have difficulty with this first-order task. DiffIPC does not converge under default settings and only runs stably after manual tuning of the solver parameters, and then needs about 26 minutes. Newton/Warp, meanwhile, fails on this task: it consumes massive memory (49 GB tape for 131k substeps) before its gradients explode through the complex dynamics simulation, resulting in random gradient signs and total optimization failure.

title: Task Setup.
text:
Task Setup.
Crucially, how large this trajectory change is depends on the stiffness of the body itself. Therefore, the trajectory sensitivity must be evaluated at a specific value of $E$ , which we set to $E^{\star}$ ( $6{\cdot}10^{4}$ Pa). The design is thus local: it finds the most informative throw for a body of roughly this stiffness, assuming a rough estimate of the stiffness is already available. To ensure robustness against launch errors, we maximize the sensitivity of the predicted rigid motion to $\log_{10}E$ , averaged over eight small perturbations of the release velocity $v_{0}$ . Because the objective itself is a derivative, maximizing it via gradient ascent fundamentally requires a second-order gradient .

title: Optimization Results.
text:
Optimization Results.
Our model supports higher-order derivatives and provides this second-order gradient directly via reverse-mode automatic differentiation. In just 30 Adam steps (7 minutes), our model successfully optimizes the throw. Replaying this designed throw in the ground-truth solver confirms its effectiveness: the sensitivity of the rigid motion to $E$ increases by $13\times$ , and per-vertex sensitivity by $1.85\times$ . This highly informative trajectory significantly widens the basin of attraction, enabling successful $E$ recovery even from a distant initial guess ( $E_{0}=10^{6}$ ) where the original throw stalls. Figure 16 visualizes the ground-truth trajectories of the initial and the optimized throw, the sensitivity gain, and the subsequent material-estimation runs from this distant initial guess.
Figure 16: Beyond material estimation: designing a more informative throw. (a) Ground-truth replays of the initial and optimized release velocities at $E^{\star}=60$ kPa. Orange and blue overlays represent stiffness perturbations of $-0.05$ and $+0.05$ dex. The first three columns show true motion at matched times and a shared camera scale. In the final column, rigid translation and rotation offsets from the nominal trajectory are magnified by $5\times$ , using equal magnification in both rows. (b) Cumulative rigid-pose sensitivity, normalized by the initial throw’s final score, increases by $13.4\times$ . This score is computed from the unamplified GT trajectories. (c) Material estimation from the same distant initial guess, $E_{0}=1{,}000$ kPa. After 60 estimation steps, the initial throw remains near $901$ kPa, whereas the optimized throw reaches $73.7$ kPa, much closer to the true $60$ kPa. Throw design uses 30 Adam steps and approximately 7 minutes.

title: Comparison with Differentiable Simulators.
text:
Comparison with Differentiable Simulators.
If the first-order task is already this challenging for existing solvers, this second-order throw design becomes infeasible for them. DiffIPC is inherently limited to first-order analytic adjoints; forcing it to approximate the necessary second-order gradient requires nested finite differences ( $64$ forward solves per step). As a result, a single gradient step takes 2.4 hours, about $635\times$ slower than our model. The whole design would therefore take about three days, which is not acceptable in practice. For Newton/Warp, which already fails to produce a usable first-order gradient, such higher-order applications are insurmountable. In contrast, PhysLDM effortlessly scales to these advanced demands, acting as a fast, stable surrogate that natively supports higher-order derivatives. Table 13 summarizes the comparison on both tasks.
